query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The degradation of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA at high temperatures is governed by the formation and stability of a protective, multi‐component oxide scale. In oxidizing environments, reactive elements (primarily Al, Ti, and Cr) form a dense, adherent oxide (predominantly Al2O3 and TiO2 mixtures) which retards oxygen diffusion into the fcc matrix and helps preserve mechanical integrity. Conversely, in reducing environments, the same elements fail to maintain a protective scale due to partial reduction or volatile suboxide formation, resulting in accelerated oxygen ingress, microstructural degradation, and embrittlement.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐fabricated additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with a homogeneous fcc matrix and minimal pre‐existing surface oxides.
generation.intervention: Expose identical specimens to an elevated temperature (e.g., 750 °C) under controlled oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Temperature set at or above 750 °C with one group in an oxygen-rich (pure O2 or air) environment and a second group in a reducing atmosphere (e.g., H2-containing or highly inert gas with minimal oxygen). The exposure time should be sufficient (on the order of 10–50 hours) to allow oxide scale formation or degradation processes to occur.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation, composition, and adhesion of the surface oxide scale, particularly the enrichment of Al, Ti, and Cr at the surface with controlled oxide phase morphology.
generation.mechanism: In the oxidizing gas environment, rapid formation of a coherent, multi-component oxide scale minimizes further oxygen ingress by presenting a diffusion barrier, preserving the underlying fcc structure and mechanical performance. In contrast, under reducing conditions, either the oxide scale does not form effectively or becomes non-protective (through partial reduction or increased porosity), leading to enhanced oxygen diffusion, microstructural degradation (such as grain boundary oxidation or internal oxidation), and resulting in reduced strength and fatigue life.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to oxidizing conditions will display a stable, thicker, and adherent oxide scale with minimal internal degradation, thereby retaining high mechanical strength and fatigue resistance relative to the as-fabricated baseline. Samples under reducing conditions will show less protective or disrupted scale formation, higher incidences of internal oxidation, and degraded mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: As-fabricated alloy with an intact fcc matrix and homogeneous elemental distribution, showing high strength and fatigue performance before any elevated-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under high-temperature conditions (around 750 °C or higher) and over exposure durations that allow significant oxide scale evolution (e.g., 10–50 hours). Results may differ if the alloy composition or processing alters the availability of reactive elements necessary for scale formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thickness, phase composition, and adhesion quality of the oxide scale in both atmospheres and the relative contributions of each reactive element (Al, Ti, Cr) to the scale’s protective behavior need further quantification. Also, the interplay with any secondary phases or precipitates formed during aging has not been fully delineated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple samples of the as-fabricated Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy and perform isothermal aging at 750 °C under two controlled environments: (a) oxidizing (pure O2 or air) and (b) reducing (H2-rich or inert with trace O2). Monitor the evolution of surface oxide scale and the internal microstructure using SEM, TEM, and atom probe tomography. Simultaneously, conduct mechanical tests (e.g., yield strength and fatigue performance) before and after exposure to assess degradation.
measurements: Surface oxide scale thickness, composition, and adhesion (via XRD, SEM, TEM)
Internal microstructural changes (grain boundary oxidation, precipitate evolution)
Residual stress distribution near the oxide/substrate interface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidizing environment does not lead to the formation of a more stable, well-adherent oxide scale with correspondingly lower degradation (or if the reducing environment shows similar protective oxide behavior and preserved mechanical properties), then the reactive element-controlled oxide scale mechanism governing degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Microstructure-Property Correlation and Its Evolution during Aging in an Al4.4Co26Cr19Fe18Ni27Ti5.6 High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe efficient energy use in multiple sectors of modern industry is partly based on the efficient use of high-strength, high-performance alloys that retain remarkable mechanical properties at elevated and high temperatures. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent the most recent class of these materials with a high potential for high-temperature high-strength applications. Aside from their chemical composition and microstructure-property relationship, limited information on the effect of heat treatment as a decisive factor for alloy design is available in the literature. This work intends to contribute to this research topic by investigating the effect of heat treatment on the microstructure and mechanical performance of an Al4.4Co26Cr19Fe18Ni27Ti5.6 HEA. The solution annealed state is compared to aged states obtained at different heat treatment times at 750 °C.
